intro: The plain-text protocol of the optical port: the small infrared window on the front of most European electricity meters. A technician puts a probe on the port, and a magnet holds it there. Laptop and meter exchange short messages in ASCII (ordinary text characters), first at 300 baud (bits per second), then faster. The meter answers with lines such as 1.8.0(012345.678*kWh): an address, a value and a unit.
plain: This is how a technician reads an electricity meter on site with a laptop. A small reader stuck to the front of the meter talks to it with flashes of invisible light, like a TV remote. The meter answers with a list of short lines, each a label, a number and a unit, much like the numbers you would copy from its display by hand. To see more or to change settings, the technician must first give a password.

signon.title: Say hello
signon.text: The technician puts the optical probe on the meter's front. The laptop sends /?!, which means "who are you?". It sends at 300 baud, with 7 data bits and an even parity bit (a simple check on each character): the settings every meter starts with. The meter answers with its maker, its top speed and its model.

select.title: Pick speed and mode
select.text: The laptop answers with an ACK (acknowledge) message. In it, the laptop picks the normal protocol, 9600 baud and a data readout: a fixed list of values that the meter sends at once. After the last byte of this message, both sides switch to 9600 baud.

readout.title: Receive the readout
readout.text: The meter sends its readout list in one message. A BCC (block check character) ends it: one byte computed from the others, so the laptop can spot a damaged message. No password is needed: the list holds only what the utility chose to show.

program.title: Programming mode
program.text: Export energy, what the building fed into the grid, is not in the list. The laptop signs on again at 300 baud and asks for programming mode. That mode can read any value and change settings, so the meter asks for a password.

password.title: Send the password
password.text: The laptop sends the password in a P1 command, in clear text: anyone watching could read it. The meter accepts it with a single ACK byte.

read.title: Read and leave
read.text: The R1 command reads one value by its address. The meter answers with the address, the value and the unit. Then the B0 command (break) ends the session, and the meter goes back to 300 baud.

frames.ident: Maker EXA, model EM340, up to 9600 baud
frames.data: 1.8.0, energy taken from the grid = 12 345.678 kWh, then tariff 1 and tariff 2
frames.ident-2: Maker EXA, model EM340, up to 9600 baud
frames.r1: Read 2.8.0, the energy fed into the grid

slash.name: Start
slash.note: / (0x2F) starts the sign-on and the identification.

end-request.name: End
end-request.note: ! (0x21) ends the request. On a line shared by several meters, the meter's address stands between ? and !.

crlf.name: CR LF
crlf.note: 0D 0A: carriage return and line feed, the end of a line.

maker.name: Maker
maker.note: EXA: the maker's three-letter code (made up here).

baud-5.name: Top speed
baud-5.note: 5: in mode C, the usual mode where laptop and meter agree on a faster speed, this meter can switch to 9600 baud. 0 would be 300 baud, 6 is 19200.

model.name: Model
model.note: EM340: the model, up to 16 characters chosen by the maker.

ack.name: ACK
ack.note: ACK (0x06) starts the acknowledgment and option select message: the laptop's choice of protocol, speed and mode.

protocol.name: Protocol
protocol.note: 0: the normal protocol. 2 would switch to HDLC and DLMS (mode E).

speed.name: Speed
speed.note: 5: switch to 9600 baud, the speed the meter offered.

mode-readout.name: Mode
mode-readout.note: 0: data readout. Right after this message, both sides switch to 9600 baud.

mode-program.name: Mode
mode-program.note: 1: programming mode. The meter will ask for a password.

stx.name: STX
stx.note: STX (0x02), start of text: the data starts. The BCC counts from the next byte.

a-180.name: Address
a-180.note: 1.8.0: active energy import (taken from the grid), all tariffs. It is the C.D.E part of the OBIS code, the address DLMS meters use for the same value.

v-180.name: Value
v-180.note: (012345.678*kWh): the value and its unit, between brackets.

v-182.name: Value
v-182.note: (003580.246*kWh). Tariff 1 and tariff 2 add up to the total.

etx.name: ETX
etx.note: ETX (0x03), end of text: the message ends. It is the last byte the BCC counts.

bcc-data.name: BCC
bcc-data.note: 0x76: every byte after STX, up to and including ETX, combined with XOR (bit by bit: equal bits give 0, different bits give 1). If it does not match, read again.

soh.name: SOH
soh.note: SOH (0x01), start of heading: a command message starts. The BCC counts from the next byte, STX included.

p0.name: P0
p0.note: The meter asks for a password, and sends an operand with it.

operand.name: Operand
operand.note: (87654321): a number chosen by the meter. A meter that wants a scrambled password (P2) uses it as a seed, the starting value of the scrambling. This one takes the password in clear text.

bcc-p0.name: BCC
bcc-p0.note: 0x68: XOR of all bytes after SOH, up to and including ETX.

p1.name: P1
p1.note: Here is the password, in clear text.

password.name: Password
password.note: (18273645). Anyone watching the optical port can read it.

bcc-p1.name: BCC
bcc-p1.note: 0x69: the check byte of this command.

ack-password.name: ACK
ack-password.note: ACK (0x06): the password is right. Reading and writing are open.

r1.name: R1
r1.note: Read one value, as ASCII text.

ask-280.name: Address
ask-280.note: 2.8.0(): the address to read, with empty brackets.

bcc-r1.name: BCC
bcc-r1.note: 0x59: the check byte of this command.

a-280.name: Address
a-280.note: 2.8.0: active energy export, all tariffs: what the building's solar panels fed into the grid.

bcc-answer.name: BCC
bcc-answer.note: 0x5F: from the byte after STX up to and including ETX.

b0.name: B0
b0.note: Break: the session ends at once.

bcc-b0.name: BCC
bcc-b0.note: 0x71, the letter q. A break is always the same 5 bytes: 01 42 30 03 71.

l-d.name: D · processing
l-d.note: 8: the total over time, so energy.

l-e.name: E · tariff
l-e.note: 0: all tariffs (price periods) together. 1.8.1 is tariff 1.

l-value.name: Value
l-value.note: 012345.678: the digits the meter keeps, with its decimal point.

facts.between: Hand-held unit or laptop → meter, through an optical probe
facts.transport: Infrared port with a magnetic probe; also a 20 mA current loop or RS-232
facts.security: None for a readout. Programming mode: a password, sent in clear
facts.speed: Starts at 300 baud, 7E1; then up to 19200 baud

tips: Set the serial port to 7 data bits and even parity (7E1). At 8N1 (8 data bits, no parity) the meter sees parity errors and stays silent, and its answers look like garbage.
Switch to the new speed only when the last byte of the ACK message has left. USB adapters hold data in a buffer: switching too early sends the end of the message at the wrong speed.
The BCC starts after STX or SOH, not with it, and it includes ETX. Getting either end wrong is a common bug in home-made readers.
